3. The Generator

blocks.alt: Random noise goes through the generator to produce generated data

blocks.text: This connects back to the decoder alone becoming a working generator, already covered in Variational Autoencoders. A GAN's own generator genuinely plays a very similar role, turning random noise into fake data.
It genuinely trains through a completely different mechanism, explored throughout the rest of this topic, rather than the KL-regularized reconstruction already covered for Variational Autoencoders.
4. The Discriminator

blocks.alt: A real or fake sample goes through the discriminator to a real/fake label

blocks.text: This connects back to the generator, already covered in this topic. A genuinely second network, the discriminator, tries to tell real data apart from the generator's own fakes.
It genuinely outputs a single probability: how likely is this input to be real, a genuinely simple binary classification task explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 5. Adversarial Training

blocks.alt: The generator competes against the discriminator

blocks.text: This connects back to the generator and discriminator, both already covered in this topic. The two networks genuinely train against each other in a direct competition.
The generator genuinely tries to fool the discriminator; the discriminator genuinely tries not to be fooled, a genuinely adversarial dynamic explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This adversarial dynamic, already covered in this topic, directly explains why GANs are named the way they are, with adversarial referring to this genuine competition between the generator and discriminator.

blocks.text: 6. The Minimax Game

blocks.alt: The generator minimizes while the discriminator maximizes in a minimax game

blocks.text: This connects back to adversarial training, already covered in this topic. This competition is genuinely framed as a minimax game between the two networks.
Genuinely one network's own gain is directly the other network's own loss, a genuinely precise mathematical framing explored throughout the rest of this topic.
7. Mode Collapse

blocks.alt: A generator produces limited variety in mode collapse

blocks.text: This connects back to the minimax game, already covered in this topic. This genuinely adversarial setup makes training famously unstable in practice.
Mode collapse, a genuinely common failure where the generator produces only a narrow range of outputs, is one real symptom, a genuinely practical challenge explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 8. GAN Versus VAE, Directly Compared
This connects back to Variational Autoencoders, already covered in Variational Autoencoders, optimizing one combined loss. GANs genuinely optimize two competing networks against each other instead.
GANs genuinely tend to produce sharper output; VAEs genuinely tend to train more stably, a genuinely real tradeoff explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.alt: Needing sharp, realistic samples points toward using a GAN

blocks.text: This connects back to genuinely needing sharp, highly realistic generated output, already covered in this topic. GANs, already covered in this topic, directly deliver exactly that sharpness.

This connects back to Variational Autoencoders, already covered, favoring genuinely more stable training instead. Variational Autoencoders, already covered, remain genuinely preferable when training stability matters more.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates the discriminator's own classification role, already covered in this topic, scoring real and fake samples.

code.content:
import random
random.seed(0)

def discriminator(x, weight=0.8, bias=-0.3):
    # already covered as outputting a probability of being real in this topic
    score = x * weight + bias
    probability_real = 1 / (1 + 2.71828 ** -score)
    return probability_real

def generator(noise, weight=1.2, bias=0.5):
    # already covered as turning random noise into fake data in this topic
    return noise * weight + bias

real_samples = [0.9, 1.0, 0.95, 1.05]  # already covered as real data in this topic
noise_samples = [random.uniform(-1, 1) for _ in range(4)]
fake_samples = [generator(n) for n in noise_samples]  # already covered as the generator's own fakes in this topic

print("Discriminator scores on real samples (already covered in this topic):")
for x in real_samples:
    print(f"  real={x:.2f} -> P(real)={discriminator(x):.3f}")

print("\nDiscriminator scores on fake samples (already covered as adversarial training in this topic):")
for x in fake_samples:
    print(f"  fake={x:.2f} -> P(real)={discriminator(x):.3f}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows the discriminator scoring real samples with generally higher probabilities than fake samples, exactly the classification task already covered in this topic, though an untrained generator still produces easily distinguishable fakes.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: GANs are a generative model family built on training two networks against each other.
The generator turns random noise into fake data, similar in role to a decoder.
The discriminator tries to tell real data apart from the generator's own fakes.
The two networks train adversarially: the generator tries to fool, the discriminator tries not to be fooled.
This competition is framed as a minimax game, where one network's gain is the other's loss.
This adversarial setup makes training famously unstable, with mode collapse a common failure.
GANs tend to produce sharper output than VAEs, which tend to train more stably instead.
GANs suit tasks needing sharp, realistic output; VAEs suit tasks needing more stable training.
